lessons.title: Phrasing: leave space instead of filling every bar
lessons.explanation: A phrase is the smallest musical unit that feels complete, and the moment you accept that definition the practical problem changes shape. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom defines the phrase as the smallest category of section, distinguished from a motive by giving the sense of completing a formal unit, and it notes that in classical music phrases end with cadences while in popular music a phrase may be completed by a melody reaching four measures in length or by completing a line of lyric, and that most phrases are four measures although five, six and seven-measure phrases occur. Open Music Theory's chapter on melody and phrasing adds the structural view: a pop or rock section consists of two, three or four phrases, and in this repertoire a phrase typically lasts four bars and corresponds to one line of the lyrics, with common patterns of aa-prime, aa-prime-b and the four-phrase statement, restatement, departure and conclusion. If a phrase is a sentence, it needs a full stop, and a full stop is made of time in which nothing is being said. That is why filling every bar with continuous notes reads as noise to a listener even when every note is correct: the boundaries that make phrases audible are created by endings, and an ending requires either a cadence, a lyric completion, a change of activity - or a rest. Space is therefore not the absence of playing; it is the material out of which phrasing is built. It also does two practical jobs at once: it lets a listener hear the other players, and it gives you a moment to hear where you actually are rather than guessing.
lessons.example: Take a 12-bar blues form at 100 beats per minute, where computed bar length is 2.4 s and each four-bar phrase lasts 9.6 s. Open Music Theory notes that 12-bar blues progressions are the most common example of a three-part aa-prime-b section, so the phrasing is already written into the form. Step one, mark the three phrases: bars one to four, five to eight, nine to twelve. Step two, allocate space before you play anything. Decide that in each four-bar phrase you will play for three beats and rest for one, which leaves 25 per cent of the phrase unhitched; alternatively decide that you will play in bars one to three and rest the first bar of the next phrase. Either rule is fine, but a rule stated in advance is what stops the space from being filled by habit. Step three, use the third phrase for the answer. In aa-prime-b the final four bars are new material that answers the repeated pair, so this is where a contrasting gesture belongs rather than more of the same. Step four, count the rests as carefully as the notes. A rest that is not counted is indistinguishable from a mistake, and a bar of silence played from the wrong beat is the most audible kind of wrong in an ensemble. Step five, listen back through a recording rather than from memory, because the experience of playing a passage and the experience of hearing it are not the same evidence. If you record, note that a MIDI part you played on a keyboard is note data rather than a captured sound, so the phrasing you judge must be judged from what the instrument or software actually produced.
lessons.question: A soloist plays continuous eighth notes across a sixteen-bar vamp, every note drawn from the right scale, and the singer says the arrangement has no shape and no room. Using the phrase definitions in the sources, which diagnosis is best?
lessons.answer: The line has no phrase boundaries: continuous notes give the listener nothing to segment, so the fix is four-bar phrasing with rests and an answering gesture rather than more correct notes
lessons.distractor: The solo is too quiet relative to the voice, so the fix is to raise it until it cuts through the texture and the shape becomes audible
lessons.correction: A phrase is defined as the smallest unit that gives a sense of completing a formal unit, and in pop music a phrase typically lasts four bars and corresponds to one lyric line, so shape comes from endings rather than from level. Thirty-two notes with no rests contain no boundary markers for the listener to use, and the second option is a level error rather than a phrasing error: raising a shapeless line makes the shapelessness louder. A phrase structure such as aa-prime-b gives the listener two hearings of an idea and then an answer, which is audible structure produced at no cost in additional notes.

depth.definitions: A phrase is the smallest category of section, a musical unit that gives the sense of completing a formal unit; in this repertoire it is typically four bars and often matches one line of lyric. A subphrase is a smaller grouping inside a phrase, and a motive is a short figure that is developed rather than completed. A cadence is the harmonic gesture that ends a phrase in classical music; pop phrases are more often closed by melodic length or lyric completion. Rest is measured silence. Density is the number of events per unit of time. Contrast is the deliberate difference between two passages; the elements used to create it include melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, dynamics and instrumentation. A functional layer is a way of grouping instruments by their role, and the novelty layer in particular works in opposition to the melodic layer through call-and-response gestures or interjections. Call and response is the alternation of a statement and an answering gesture. Prerequisites: phrase writing from lesson 46, form boundaries from lesson 47, and the rhythmic consistency of lesson 53.
depth.mechanism: Hearing is segmentation: a listener groups a stream of events into units by using boundaries, and boundaries are detected where one or more musical parameters change at once. That is why a rest is powerful: it changes density to zero, which is an unmistakable boundary marker, and it does so without requiring a chord change or a dynamic shift. Two further mechanisms matter. The first is that space makes other parts audible: if two instruments occupy the same register and the same rhythmic slots, their attacks coincide and neither can be heard as phrasing, whereas a gap in one part exposes the shape of the other. The second is attention: a player who is playing continuously has no time to listen, and an ensemble loses the reciprocal prediction and adaptation that keeps time together. Space therefore improves both the listener's experience of structure and the player's ability to stay in the music. The limitation to state honestly is that space is not automatically musical; silence in the wrong place, or silence that is not counted, creates a hole rather than a phrase ending, which is why the rule must be written in bars rather than felt per moment.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two arrangements of the same sixteen bars. In the first, keyboard and guitar both sustain full chords through every bar while a vocal line or lead instrument plays above them; every layer is always present, so the texture never changes and the sixteenth bar sounds like the first. In the second, the same parts are assigned to functional roles. The chordal instruments drop out for the first two bars of each four-bar phrase and enter on beat one of bar three, the bass holds the pulse, and the lead instrument answers in the space - the arrangement the source describes as a novelty layer working in opposition to a melodic layer through call-and-response. The notes played in the second version are fewer and the perceived structure is larger, because the listener can hear four statements of an idea rather than one unbroken surface. A third case is the four-part pattern the source calls statement, restatement, departure and conclusion: the third phrase is where the departure belongs, often with an accelerated harmonic rhythm and movement away from the tonic, and putting continuous activity there instead erases the one place in the section where a listener expects a change.
depth.mistake: The misconception that causes the most damage is that stopping means failing to play, so a rest is experienced as a gap that must be apologised for. The diagnostic is to play a four-bar phrase twice, once with continuous eighths and once with the final beat silent, and ask which version a listener could describe back to you; if the silent version is more describable, the space is doing structural work and not covering a deficiency. A second mistake is equating space with long notes: holding one note for four bars is not phrasing, it is an absence of information, and it produces the same listener problem as continuous notes. A third is resting by stopping to think, which reads as hesitation because the silence has no known length; a rest is only a rest when it has a measured duration. A fourth is judging the result from memory while playing, which is unreliable for the same reason a singer cannot judge their own balance from inside their own head.
depth.application: Task in two passes over a sixteen-bar vamp, one 20-minute session with a two-minute warm-up, at a comfortable volume. Before playing, write a phrase plan in bars: four phrases of four bars, the specific bars in which you will rest, and one sentence describing what the answering gesture in the fourth phrase will do differently from the first. Pass one: play continuous activity and note how it feels. Pass two: play the written plan, counting the rests aloud under your breath. Then write three observations: which pass a listener would be able to describe, whether the rests were counted rather than felt, and what changed in your awareness of the other parts. Model response for a sixteen-bar vamp at 100 beats per minute, where a four-bar phrase is 9.6 s: plan of four phrases; rest on beat four of each phrase, which is 1 of 16 beats or about 6 per cent of the section, plus one whole silent bar in phrase three, another 6 per cent; pass one felt busy and I lost count twice; pass two was steadier and I heard the bass line's repeated figure for the first time. Self-review rubric: one point for a phrase plan written in bars before playing, one for rests that were on the beat, one for naming a structural consequence rather than a comfort, one for a specific observation about another part. Warm up, keep the session under half an hour, and if you monitor with headphones keep the level low enough to hear the room.
depth.summary: Phrasing is the deliberate arrangement of statements and endings, and space is the material that supplies the endings. A player who writes a four-bar phrase plan, rests inside it on purpose, and answers rather than overlaps will sound structured even when playing fewer notes than before, and the same discipline transfers to comping, to accompanying a singer, and to arranging where the parts themselves take turns.

lessons.title: Record a part cleanly and judge the take honestly
lessons.explanation: Recording is a two-part skill: capturing a part accurately, and then listening to what you captured without confusing it with what you remember playing. The capture side is mostly preparation. In a project there is a difference between capturing sound and capturing performance data: the FL Studio Transport Panel's Recording Filter separates Notes, which records note data from a keyboard or drum pads, from Audio, which records sound, so choosing the wrong category means you have either no sound or nothing to edit. The judgement side is where most learners lose the benefit of recording. A review of feedback interventions in piano teaching states that students' self-evaluation of their own performances agrees less with expert ratings than experts' own judgements, that accuracy of self-assessment improves with maturity and expertise, and that self-recordings are considered valuable feedback precisely because they raise awareness of what was actually played. Practical recording literature supplies the other half of the method: keep every take while tracking, aim for about three complete takes of a part rather than dozens of fragments, record without effects where possible because reverb and delay gloss over timing and intonation, and judge takes against a written criterion instead of a feeling of confidence. Put together, that is a repeatable routine: prepare the capture, keep the takes, then audition them with criteria and at matched levels, preferably after an interval.
lessons.example: Take a 32-bar part at 100 beats per minute. Computed here rather than measured: one bar is 2.4 s, so the part lasts 76.8 s and three complete takes hold 230.4 s of material, about 3 minutes 50 seconds, of which you will keep one third. Step one, prepare the capture. Decide the category first: a keyboard performance intended to be editable later should be captured as note data, while a guitar or voice is sound and has to be captured as audio. Set a level with headroom, so the loudest moment is not clipping, and check that you can hear both yourself and the other material without turning anything up loud - if the level has to be raised to hear detail, the room or the monitoring is the problem. Step two, record with a count-in, keeping every take rather than deleting as you go, because the take you dislike while playing may be the one that holds together when heard. Step three, audition with criteria and paper. Score each take on four lines: timing against the pulse, pitch or intonation, tone and level consistency, and whether the musical intention survived. Listen to each take twice - once only for timing, once for everything else - and match the playback levels of the takes, because a louder take sounds better than an equally good quieter one. Step four, use the grid as a reference rather than a verdict: at 100 beats per minute the sixteenth-note grid is 0.15 s, so a note displaced by a sixteenth is a different rhythm and not merely a loose performance. Step five, sleep on it if you can and re-audition the next day. Students' self-evaluation is known to be less accurate than experts' judgements and to improve with experience, so give yourself the best chance the method allows: criteria, matched levels, repetition, and an interval.
lessons.question: A learner records a take, listens once, decides it is good, and an experienced player later points out that one phrase is late and another is out of tune. Which change to the learner's process is best supported by the evidence cited in this lesson?
lessons.answer: Audition every take with written criteria in more than one listening pass at matched levels and with an interval before deciding, because self-evaluation of one's own performance is less accurate than expert judgement and improves with practice
lessons.distractor: Trust the first listening impression, because repeated listening to a performance makes the ear progressively less objective and the initial reaction is the most reliable
lessons.correction: The feedback literature reports that students' self-evaluations agree less with expert ratings than experts' judgements do, and that self-assessment accuracy improves with maturity and experience, while self-recordings are valued as feedback for the awareness they raise. That argues for a method that compensates - criteria, repeated passes, matched playback levels and a delay - rather than for trusting a single impression. A second listening pass is not a loss of objectivity; the documented failure is the absence of any structured listening at all.

depth.definitions: A take is one complete attempt at a part. An overdub is a part recorded on top of existing material; a drop-in or punch-in replaces a section inside an existing take. Comping is compiling one finished performance from several takes. In FL Studio the safest recording mode keeps all takes rather than discarding earlier ones, and takes recorded in a loop are written to the Playlist as separate audio clips. Note data is performance information - which note, when, how hard - and is not sound; audio is a captured waveform of sound. Monitoring is what you hear of yourself and of the material while recording. Headroom is the space between the loudest moment and the ceiling where the signal distorts. Self-evaluation is a judgement about your own performance; a rubric is a written list of criteria used for that judgement. Prerequisites: the count-in work of lesson 63, the honest recording routine of lesson 37, and the loudness and balance judgement of lesson 49.
depth.mechanism: Judging a take is difficult because the memory of playing it competes with what the recording contains. While playing, attention is spread across execution, listening and coordination, so the experience of a performance is dominated by motor effort rather than by the resulting sound. Listening to a recording moves the judgement to an external observer position, which is why the feedback literature treats self-recording as a tool for raising awareness rather than as a convenience. Two biases then need managing. The first is level bias: a louder take is consistently heard as better, so comparisons must be made at matched levels. The second is familiarity bias: having just played a phrase, you hear the intention rather than the sound, which is why an interval between take and judgement helps. The independent variable you control is the quality of the criteria, so criteria should name things that can be heard independently - timing against the pulse, intonation, consistency of tone and level, and whether the shape of the phrase survived - rather than global words such as good or tight.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the same part captured two ways. Captured as note data, the take is editable per note: a late note can be moved, a hard note softened, the tempo adjusted, and the sound changed entirely by choosing another instrument, which means the instrumental tone is not part of the judgement at all and the only questions are timing, dynamics and note choice. Captured as audio, the take fixes everything that happened: the attack, the room, the tuning, the noise, and the human timing as a waveform, so editing timing requires time-stretching or slicing the waveform, and each slice risks a click unless a fade is used. The judgement criteria must change accordingly: for note data, ask whether the performance would still be musical on any instrument; for audio, ask whether the tone and the room are part of what you want. A third contrast concerns effects. Recording with reverb and delay in place makes the take easier to like and harder to judge, because those effects smear timing and pitch differences; the same take recorded dry exposes its problems immediately, which is uncomfortable and useful.
depth.mistake: The most expensive habit is the take spiral: recording again and again past the point where the performance is improving, which produces dozens of fragments, fatigue, and no decision. Practical recording guidance recommends aiming for roughly three complete takes of a part and warns against keeping very large numbers of takes in order to choose the best one later. A second mistake is comparing takes without matching their playback levels, which reliably selects the loudest. A third is judging a take on the day it was played, when the memory of effort is strongest, and never revisiting it. A fourth, specific to projects, is capturing a keyboard performance as audio when note data was wanted, which converts an editable performance into a fixed waveform; the diagnostic is to ask, before recording, whether you want to be able to change a note afterwards. If yes, that part is note data.
depth.application: Task, one session of 25 to 30 minutes including setup, at a low monitoring level and with a two-minute warm-up first. Record three complete takes of one eight-bar part, keeping all three. Then write the rubric before listening: timing against the pulse, intonation, consistency of tone and level, and survival of the phrase shape, each scored out of five. Audition the takes at matched levels, twice each, once for timing only and once for everything else, and write the scores down. Choose one take, and write two sentences explaining the choice using the rubric rather than adjectives alone. Model response: 'Take two scored 4 for timing, 4 for intonation, 3 for consistency and 4 for shape; take three scored 5 for consistency but 2 for timing because the second phrase pushed; take two wins because the rhythmic anchor is the part the arrangement needs and the level inconsistency is the easiest defect to correct.' Self-review rubric: one point for criteria written before listening, one for matched levels, one for two separate passes, one for a decision justified against a named criterion rather than a preference. Protect your hearing: set the monitor level before you begin and leave it alone, take a short break every 20 to 25 minutes, and if your ears ring after a session, the level was too high, not the material too quiet.
depth.summary: Clean capture is a preparation problem and honest judgement is a method problem. Decide whether you are recording sound or performance data, record with a count-in, keep your takes, and then audition them against written criteria at matched levels in more than one pass, ideally after an interval. That routine transfers to every future recording, and it is the one that makes the difference between a folder of takes and a decision you can defend.

lessons.title: Edit without destroying the performance: cuts, fades and what not to fix
lessons.explanation: Editing a recorded performance is mostly the discipline of doing less than you could. Every cut in an audio waveform is a discontinuity, and a discontinuity is heard as a click unless it is handled: the FL Studio manual's Audio Clips page documents exactly the tools for handling it, including a crossfade control, automatic crossfades set in the Playlist project settings, fade handles, a create-crossfade command for overlapping clips, and a set of declicking options, with a reminder that if finer control is needed the snap setting can be turned off. Recording practice literature adds the priorities that keep an edit from becoming an arrangement: record without effects if you plan to comp, because reverb and delay cover the very timing and tuning problems you are trying to hear, use short crossfades to smooth the joins, keep the number of takes small, and prefer retaking a whole section over chains of tiny drop-ins. The general rule that follows from both is: cut where the music is already quiet, keep the cuts few, and repair the smallest thing that actually needs repairing. Editing is not a second performance; it is a series of interventions in one, and each intervention costs some of the original. The skill is knowing when the cost exceeds the benefit - which is usually whenever the edit is audible as an edit, and always when the repair is being used to avoid re-recording something that simply was not played well enough.
lessons.example: Take a guitar part recorded as two complete takes over 32 bars at 100 beats per minute, where each take is 76.8 s and the sixteenth-note grid is 0.15 s (computed; the grid is not a perceptual threshold, just the finest division the project displays). Step one, keep a copy. Duplicate the takes before touching anything, so that a failed edit can be abandoned rather than reversed. Step two, plan the cuts at phrase boundaries rather than by ear alone: with four-bar phrases, that is eight phrases over the form, which is where the natural gaps between gestures already exist. Step three, use short fades rather than hard edges. A 10 ms fade at 44.1 kHz spans 441 samples and a 5 ms fade spans 221 samples, so eight crossfades at 10 ms cost 80 ms of the performance in total, which is small next to a 150 ms sixteenth. That arithmetic is the reason short fades are the default: they remove the click without changing the rhythm you can hear. Step four, cut in the gaps. If a cut must fall inside a sustained note, expect the envelope to be altered, because the note's natural decay is what the cut removes; moving the cut to the nearest 0.15 s of silence preserves the sound. Step five, listen for the artefacts you created, not for the ones you were trying to fix: click, thump, truncated decay, and any place where the timing jumps because the two takes were played at slightly different feels. If there are more than a couple of such places, the correct action is to re-record the section rather than to keep splicing.
lessons.question: A learner slices a two-take guitar performance note by note, moves each note onto the sixteenth-note grid, uses long crossfades to hide the joins, and finds that the result clicks anyway and sounds mechanical. Which reading of the problem is best supported by the sources in this lesson?
lessons.answer: The cuts created discontinuities and the long fades smeared the envelope, while moving notes off their played positions removed the timing that made the part musical: the fix is fewer cuts in the gaps, short fades, and leaving the played timing alone
lessons.distractor: The clicks come from too few cuts, so the waveform should be divided into even smaller segments and each segment faded separately to give the fades more places to work
lessons.correction: A click is a discontinuity in the waveform, not a shortage of cuts: the documented remedy is to handle each join with a short fade or crossfade and to prefer cutting where the music is already quiet, and the Audio Clips documentation treats crossfades and declicking as the tools for exactly this. Longer fades do not remove the discontinuity more thoroughly; they alter the envelope of the sound around the join, which is why the result sounds smeared rather than clean. Meanwhile, the timing that was audible as groove was in the played note positions, so moving notes onto a grid is a change to the performance rather than a repair to it.

depth.definitions: An edit is a change to recorded material: a cut, a move, a fade, a level change or a replacement. A crossfade is the overlapping fade-out and fade-in used where two clips meet, so that the sum has no discontinuity. Declicking options apply short fades automatically at clip boundaries to remove the step in the waveform that produces a click. Slip editing moves the audio inside a fixed region without changing the region's length. Quantisation in note data moves events onto a grid; quantisation of audio requires time-stretching or slicing, which alters the waveform. A comp is one performance compiled from several takes. A destructive edit changes the recorded file; a non-destructive edit changes only the project's description of how the file is played. Prerequisites: quantisation and groove judgement from lesson 38, the count-in and take-keeping routine of lessons 63 and 68, and the arrangement habits of lesson 59.
depth.mechanism: Edits are audible when they change something the ear is using as information. Three mechanisms matter here. The first is waveform continuity: a hard cut between two samples that do not meet produces a step, and a step is a click; a short fade or crossfade removes the step because the amplitude passes continuously from one to the other, and the reason short is safe is arithmetic - 10 ms against a 150 ms sixteenth at 100 beats per minute is a fifteenth of the shortest subdivision the grid shows, so it cannot restructure the rhythm. The second is envelope integrity: a plucked or struck note has an attack and a decay, and a cut inside it removes part of the decay, which the ear hears as an unnatural truncation even if it is click-free. The third is timing information: in a performance, the small deviations from the grid are part of the groove that lesson 38 discussed, so aligning them away can convert a performance into a sequence. The reason this matters in note data far less is that moving a note in a piano roll relocates an instruction that will be rendered again, whereas moving a note in audio relocates a fragment of sound that already contains its attack and decay.
depth.secondExample: Contrast repairing a late note in a keyboard part recorded as note data with repairing the same note in an audio recording of the same performance. In note data, the note is a pair of numbers - when and how hard - so moving it is exact, reversible, and free of artefacts, and the resulting sound is regenerated by the instrument. In audio, the same repair means splitting the waveform on both sides of the note, moving the middle fragment, and covering both new joins with fades; the sound carries its recorded attack and decay, so a moved note can have a slightly different relationship to the room tone and to the note before it, and each join risks a click if the fade is missed. A third case is the compromise edit: leaving the performance whole but replacing a single short phrase from another take. That is usually the cheapest intervention, because the phrase has natural boundaries, and it is the reason the practical guidance recommends cutting on phrases rather than on single notes. The most expensive edit is the one that removes the evidence of the recording: a heavily aligned, fade-covered part that no longer has the timing anyone played.
depth.mistake: The mistake with the highest cost is treating editing as a substitute for playing well: the learner knows there is an editing stage and therefore accepts a performance that was never secure, then spends an evening splicing single notes. The diagnostic is to count the interventions required. If a part needs repairs at more than a couple of points, the practical guidance is to retake the whole section rather than to continue with micro-repairs, because each additional cut removes a little more of the original performance and each new join is another chance of a click. A second mistake is using long crossfades as insurance, which smears the envelope and can produce a gap in the sound where two fades overlap. A third is editing without keeping a copy of the raw takes, which makes experimentation risky and therefore timid. A fourth is judging the edit at a very high monitoring level: artefacts and level changes alike are exaggerated for the first twenty minutes and your ears fatigue, so check the result at a moderate level and again after a break.
depth.application: Task, one session of 25 minutes at a moderate monitoring level, with a two-minute ear-and-hand break halfway. Take the two best takes of one eight-bar part and duplicate them before editing anything. Plan the cuts on paper first: how many, and where they fall relative to notes and to phrases. Then make the comp using the fewest cuts that solve the musical problem, with short fades at every join, and listen once for the music and once only for artefacts. Write four numbers and one sentence: number of cuts, number of fades, total fade time in milliseconds, whether any cut fell inside a note, and which single cut contributed most. Model response: 'three cuts, all at phrase boundaries in the gaps, six fades of about 10 ms each, total about 60 ms, no cut inside a note; the cut at bar five repaired a mistimed entry and the other two were unnecessary, so next time I would keep two.' Self-review rubric: one point for a written cut plan before editing, one for short fades on every join, one for keeping the raw takes, one for a self-evaluation that identifies a cut you did not need. Keep the monitor level fixed, and rest your ears as well as your hands: the ear is the tool you are using for the judgement, and it degrades before you notice.
depth.summary: Editing is a set of small, deliberate interventions whose cost is measured in the originality of the performance. Cut where the music is already quiet, keep the cuts few, fade every join briefly, keep a copy of the raw material, and re-record rather than splice when the performance was not secure to begin with. The same judgement transfers to comping, to repairing a note in software, and to deciding when a part is finished.

visual.description: Plan the cuts, fade the joins, and measure what the edit cost the original.

Plan the cuts on paper and put them at phrase boundaries or in gaps: at 100 beats per minute the sixteenth grid is 0.15 s.

Audition twice, once for the music and once only for artefacts, then count your cuts and ask how many were necessary.

lessons.title: Capstone: three takes, one chosen take, and a written reason you can defend
lessons.explanation: This lesson is the level's capstone, and it asks for something narrower than a finished song: three complete takes of one part, one chosen take, and a written reason for the choice. The constraint is the method. Recording three takes rather than one gives you a decision to make, and stopping at three prevents the take spiral in which dozens of fragments remove the need to decide anything. Writing the reason converts a preference into an evaluation: the practical recording literature recommends keeping complete takes and judging between them, while the practice research is blunt about what makes judgement improve - in the study of pianists learning a difficult passage, retention quality was not significantly related to practice time, total trials or complete trials, but was related to the percentage of trials performed correctly and to the number of trials performed incorrectly, and the paper criticises the tradition of assigning practice in minutes rather than in goals. A written reason is the goal-based form of the same idea: it forces the criteria to exist before the takes do. Preparation matters too, and it is the part that separates musicians from engineers. Practical guidance suggests front-loading the technical work, documenting the setup so it can be reproduced, and arranging to control the recording without leaving your instrument, because pressing record, walking across the room and picking up a guitar each time is a reliable way to spoil the third take. Finally, deliver the piece to somebody: a rendered audio file and one honest paragraph about what it is and what it is not.
lessons.example: Specification, with all arithmetic computed here rather than measured from any file: choose a 32-bar part at 100 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.4 s and the part is 76.8 s. Step one, write the criteria before recording. Four lines are enough: timing against the pulse, intonation, consistency of tone and level, and whether the intended shape of the phrases survived. Step two, prepare and document. Set the levels once, note them down, mark positions, and arrange to start and stop recording from where you play. Step three, record exactly three complete takes, using a count-in and keeping all three: three takes at 76.8 s each hold 230.4 s, or 3 minutes 50 seconds of material, of which the chosen take will be one third. Step four, audit. Play the three takes at matched levels, twice each - one pass for timing, one for everything else - and score them on paper. Step five, choose and justify in writing: name the criterion that decided the choice, say what each rejected take did better than the chosen one, and state the single thing you would fix with more time. A useful example of a defensible justification: 'Take two had the steadiest eighth-note pulse, which is the criterion the arrangement depends on; take three was better in tone on the second phrase; take one was best in shape but drifted late by the last four bars; with more time I would re-record the last phrase only.' Step six, deliver. Render an audio file - a WAV at 16-bit stereo, 44.1 kHz, is about 12.92 MB for 76.8 s, computed - and check that the render covers what you intend it to cover, since the default renders the Master mixer track and ignores material that does not reach it. Then listen on one other system at a moderate level and write the delivery paragraph: what the part is, whether it is note data or recorded sound, what you decided and why, and what is still unresolved.
lessons.question: A learner exports a project as a MIDI file to send to a friend, and the friend reports that the file makes no sound anywhere they open it. What does the software documentation say is happening?
lessons.answer: The export is note data rather than sound: the manual states that a MIDI file saves piano-roll and step-sequencer note data and that MIDI is not an audio format, so an audio render such as a WAV is required to hear anything
lessons.distractor: The MIDI file is a compressed audio format that needs a matching codec installed before it will play
lessons.correction: The export documentation lists audio formats - WAV, MP3, OGG, FLAC and M4A - as saving an audio mix of the project, and lists MIDI separately: a .mid file saves step-sequencer and piano-roll note data to a standard MIDI file, and the manual adds explicitly that MIDI is not an audio format. A MIDI file therefore contains instructions to play notes and requires an instrument or a synthesiser to become sound. The same distinction applies inside the project: a keyboard performance captured as note data is performance information, while a guitar or voice captured through an input is recorded sound.

depth.definitions: A take is one complete attempt at a part. A comp is one performance compiled from several takes. A render or export is the act of turning a project into a file; the default render covers the Master mixer track unless individual tracks are exported separately. Bit depth describes how much resolution each sample has, and the manual's guidance is that 16-bit integer is enough for music distribution while 24 or 32-bit are for archiving production files. A MIDI file stores note data rather than sound. A delivery note is a short written statement accompanying a finished file describing what it contains and what it does not. A rubric is a written list of criteria used for evaluation. Self-evaluation is judgement about your own performance, the accuracy of which improves with experience. Prerequisites: the honest take audit of lesson 68, the edit discipline of lesson 69, and the finish-and-deliver routine of lesson 50.
depth.mechanism: The value of three takes plus a written reason comes from converting taste into measurement. Left unconstrained, take selection is dominated by three biases: recency, since the last take is the one best remembered; effort, since the take that felt hardest feels earned; and level, since louder takes are heard as better and are easily the loudest. Written criteria declared before the first take defeat recency and effort by fixing the question in advance, and matched playback levels defeat the third. The practice research supplies the reason to trust this method rather than a feeling: in the observed pianists, how much they practised was unrelated to how well they retained the passage, while the percentage of attempts played correctly was related. That does not mean time is worthless; it means the useful record is about quality of execution, which is exactly what a scored three-take audit produces. The second mechanism is transfer: a written justification is a reusable artefact, because the same four criteria can be applied to the next part, and after a few projects you have a personal record of which criteria your playing typically fails.
depth.secondExample: Compare two learners finishing the same task. The first rehearses for forty minutes, records twelve takes, keeps the loudest, and delivers a file with the note 'final take'. The second writes four criteria, prepares and documents the setup, records exactly three takes, scores them at matched levels in two passes, and delivers a file with the note: 'chosen take two, on the timing criterion; take three was stronger in tone and take one stronger in shape; the last phrase of take two is the weakest link and is the first thing I would re-record; the keyboard part is note data, the guitar is recorded audio.' Both learners have spent comparable time. Only the second has produced something another musician can act on, and only the second has a record that will shorten the next session. A third contrast is the delivery itself. Delivering a WAV that is 12.92 MB for 76.8 s at 16-bit stereo, 44.1 kHz, computed here, with a note that says what is edited and what is not, is a professional-sized handover in miniature: the recipient knows what they have and knows what to check.
depth.mistake: The mistake this capstone is designed to catch is selecting a take without criteria and then writing a reason that describes the selection instead of justifying it. The diagnostic is to read your own sentence and ask whether it could have justified a different take just as well; if it could, it is a preference in disguise. A second mistake is judging the takes at their original levels, which selects the loudest. A third is judging on the day of recording only, when the memory of effort is strongest; the honest method includes an interval and a second listening pass. A fourth is delivering a file without checking what the render contains: a default render includes the Master mixer track and omits anything that does not reach it, and the render length follows the time selection, the last marker beyond the last bar containing data, or the end of the song - so a bounce can be short, long or missing a track through no fault of the performance. A fifth is claiming more than was done. If a part was played but nothing was recorded, or a project was built but nothing was rendered, say so plainly; the honest statement is worth more than the impression of a finished production.
depth.application: Capstone task, in three sittings of no more than 30 minutes each, with a break between them. Sitting one, preparation and criteria: warm up for two minutes, set and document your levels, arrange control of the recording so you do not have to leave the instrument between takes, and write the four criteria down before playing a note. Sitting two, capture: record exactly three complete takes of the part with a count-in, keeping all three, and stop at three. Sitting three, audit, choose, deliver: score each take at matched levels in two passes with an interval, choose one, write the justification using the four-part form below, render an audio file, and listen to it on one other system at a moderate level. Write-up format, four sentences: (1) the criterion that decided the choice; (2) what each rejected take did better; (3) the single weakest moment in the chosen take and what you would do about it; (4) what the file contains - which parts are note data and which are recorded sound, and whether anything was edited. Model response for the part described in this lesson: criterion, timing, because the arrangement rests on the eighth-note pulse; rejected takes, tone on the second phrase and phrase shape overall; weakest moment, the last four bars drift late, and I would re-record that phrase alone; contents, keyboard as note data, guitar as audio, two cuts made at phrase boundaries with short fades, nothing yet rendered. Self-review rubric: one point for criteria written before recording, one for exactly three complete takes, one for matched-level scoring in two passes, one for a justification that names a criterion and concedes what the rejected takes did better, one for a delivery statement that is accurate about what the file contains. Safety throughout: warm up before playing, keep each sitting under 30 minutes with breaks, set the monitor level once and leave it alone, and if your ears ring afterwards, lower the level rather than enduring it. Nothing in this lesson has been recorded, rendered or listened to by the author: the figures are computed arithmetic, and the performance and the audition are yours to carry out.
depth.summary: The capstone compresses the whole level into one habit: decide what good sounds like before you record, capture a small number of complete takes, judge them against stated criteria at matched levels, write down why you chose what you chose, and hand the result over with an honest description of what it is. That habit is the level's real deliverable, because it is the part that transfers to every later piece, to every ensemble you play in, and to every recording you will ever judge, including your own.

visual.description: Criteria first, three takes, a scored audit, a defensible choice, and an honest delivery.
steps: Write four criteria before playing: timing, intonation, consistency of tone and level, and survival of the phrase shape.
Prepare and document the setup, and arrange recording control so you do not leave the instrument between takes.

questions.prompt: A player improvises over an eight-bar Am7 to D7 vamp using A minor pentatonic, A C D E G, and wants one note that can be held across the chord change and sound settled in both halves. Which note does that job, and why?
questions.answer: C, because it is the flat third of Am7 and also the flat seventh of D7, so it is a chord tone in both halves
questions.distractor: G, because it is the fifth above the A root and the fifth is stable against any chord in the same key
questions.correction: Inside the A minor pentatonic the Am7 chord tones are A, C, E and G, while over D7 the chord tones present in the scale are D, A and C; C therefore belongs to both chords and can be sustained across the change. G is the flat seventh of Am7 and the eleventh of D7, so it changes function too, but it is not the fifth of D7 - the fifth of D is A. Naming which pentatonic tones are chord tones of each half is the reliable way to choose a pivot note.

questions.prompt: Over a sixteen-bar vamp, a soloist plays only in bars one to three of every four-bar phrase and rests for the fourth bar, counting the rests aloud throughout. Using the phrase definitions in this level, what is the structural result and what proportion of the section is silent?
questions.answer: Four bars are silent, which is 25 per cent of the section, and each four-bar phrase ends with an audible boundary that gives the listener a unit to group
questions.distractor: Four bars are silent, which is about 12.5 per cent of the section, and the rests mainly serve to make the solo easier to play rather than to shape the form
questions.correction: Four bars out of sixteen is 25 per cent, not 12.5 per cent. More importantly, a phrase is defined as the smallest unit that gives a sense of completing a formal unit, and in pop music a phrase typically lasts four bars, so ending each phrase with a measured rest supplies the boundary the listener uses to segment the music. The rests are structural material rather than a concession to difficulty, which is why they are counted rather than felt.

questions.prompt: A learner records three takes of the same part. Take three is recorded 2 dB louder than take one and feels more exciting on playback, so the learner keeps it, noting that it had more energy. Using the evidence and methods in this level, what is wrong with the procedure?
questions.answer: The takes were compared at their original levels, so the louder take had an advantage: matched-level comparison plus written criteria in more than one pass is what makes the judgement defensible
questions.distractor: Nothing: a performance that is more exciting on playback is by definition the better performance, and energy is the criterion that matters most
questions.correction: Level bias is a predictable judgement error, and it is why the evaluation method requires matched playback levels before takes are compared. The sources also report that students' self-evaluations of their own performances agree less with expert ratings than experts' judgements do, and that self-assessment accuracy improves with experience, which argues for criteria, repeated passes and an interval rather than for trusting a first impression of energy. Energy is not a criterion until it is defined as something hearable, such as consistency of attack or the survival of the phrase shape.

questions.prompt: A two-take guitar part needs twelve repairs, mostly single notes that arrived late, and the learner plans to slice each late note out, move it, and use long crossfades to smooth the joins. What does the recording and editing material in this level recommend instead?
questions.answer: Use the fewest cuts at phrase boundaries in the gaps with short fades, and re-record the section rather than making a chain of micro-repairs when a part needs more than a couple of them
questions.distractor: Slice the part into more and smaller segments so that each join has a shorter distance to cover, and lengthen each crossfade until the clicks disappear
questions.correction: Practical comping guidance recommends keeping the intervention count low, cutting on phrases, using short crossfades, and retaking a whole section rather than chaining micro drop-ins, and the software documentation treats crossfades and declicking as the tools for joins rather than as a remedy for too many of them. Twelve repairs on one part is a performance problem rather than an editing problem: more cuts and longer fades add artefacts and remove more of the original timing without addressing why the notes arrived late.

questions.prompt: A learner finishes the capstone, deletes the two rejected takes, writes 'take three, it felt the best' as the reason, and states that the piece has been rendered although no file was ever produced. Which revision makes the submission match the level's requirements?
questions.answer: Keep all three takes, replace the reason with a named criterion plus what the rejected takes did better, and describe the file accurately, including whether any render exists at all
questions.distractor: Keep the single chosen take to save space, keep the reason as written because feeling is the only honest report of a performance, and describe the project as finished
questions.correction: The capstone requires three complete takes precisely so that a comparison can be made, a written justification that names the criterion that decided the choice and concedes what the rejected takes did better, and a delivery statement that is accurate about what exists. Deleting the rejected takes destroys the evidence for the choice, 'it felt the best' is a preference rather than a criterion, and claiming a render that was never made is a factual error about the deliverable. Note data and recorded sound should also be distinguished in the delivery note, since a keyboard part captured as note data is not a recording of sound.

questions.prompt: A quartet reads a 32-bar AABA chart at 90 beats per minute. They agree on a four-click count-in, and one player starts playing on the fourth click rather than after it. Computed from those figures, how long is one performance of the form, how long is the count-in, and what is the starting player's error in seconds?
questions.answer: The form lasts 85.333 s, the count-in lasts 2.667 s, and starting on the fourth click puts that player one beat, 0.667 s, early
questions.distractor: The form lasts 80.0 s, the count-in lasts 2.0 s, and starting on the fourth click is correct because the count-in's final click is the downbeat
questions.correction: At 90 beats per minute one beat is 60 / 90 = 0.667 s, so one 4/4 bar is 2.667 s, four clicks take 2.667 s, and 32 bars take 32 x 2.667 = 85.333 s. The count-in describes beats rather than a starting signal, so the first downbeat of the form arrives after the fourth click, and a player who begins on that click is 0.667 s early and will sound a beat ahead of everyone who waited.

questions.prompt: A lead sheet contains an eight-bar A section with a repeat sign, then an eight-bar B section, at 96 beats per minute. A player counts the phrases to plan entries. How many bars are performed, how many four-bar phrases does that give, and how long is the whole form?
questions.answer: 24 bars performed across six four-bar phrases, lasting 24 x 2.5 = 60.0 s
questions.distractor: 16 bars performed across four four-bar phrases, lasting 16 x 2.5 = 40.0 s, because repeats do not add bars to the form
questions.correction: The repeat means the A section is played twice, so the performed form is 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 bars, which is six phrases of four bars. At 96 beats per minute one beat is 0.625 s and a bar is 2.5 s, so the form is 60.0 s and a single phrase is 10.0 s. Road map information applies to the whole performance, and the phrase count is what a player uses to place entries and rests.

questions.prompt: Two players rehearse a duet. Each uses headphones that carry mostly their own instrument, both are accurate alone, and together the tempo drifts by about one and a half seconds over the form. Which change is best supported by the ensemble-timing evidence and by the recording practice in this level?
questions.answer: Change the monitoring so each player hears the other clearly, since removing feedback about a partner's performance reduces synchronization and adaptation, and agree who owns the pulse before playing
questions.distractor: Increase individual metronome practice at the agreed tempo and keep the monitoring as it is, because each player's internal clock is what determines ensemble timing
questions.correction: The duet research reports that removing auditory feedback about a partner's performance leads to reduced synchronization and adaptation, and that players adapt more to a partner's timing when they cannot hear themselves - so the feedback loop, not personal discipline, is what has been broken. The drift figure of about one and a half seconds over 32 bars is the arithmetic of two spontaneous rates being 2 to 3 beats per minute apart, which adaptation would absorb and isolation cannot. More private metronome work is useful, but it does not create the reciprocal prediction that ensemble timing depends on.

questions.prompt: A learner practises a difficult passage for forty minutes and makes ten complete runs, two of which contain an error. The session rule was nine correct runs out of ten before raising the tempo. Using the practice evidence and the capstone's requirement of stated criteria, what is the correct next action and why?
questions.answer: Stay at the current tempo or drop a rung until at least nine of ten runs are clean, because the percentage of correct trials rather than the time or the number of trials was what related to retention quality
questions.distractor: Raise the tempo immediately, because forty minutes and ten complete runs is a full session and the two errors were small
questions.correction: Eight of ten correct runs is 80 per cent, below the 90 per cent the rule requires. The underlying study found no significant relationship between retention and practice time, total trials or complete trials, while the percentage of trials performed correctly and the number of incorrect trials did relate to retention quality, so the error rate is the measure that carries information. Raising the tempo at 80 per cent adds incorrect repetitions of the passage, which is the one recorded quantity that went the wrong way. Keep the honest limit in view: the study involved seventeen pianists and one passage, so this is a hypothesis your own records should test.

questions.prompt: A soloist improvises over a sixteen-bar Am7 to D7 vamp using A minor pentatonic and fills every bar with eighths. A listener asks for more shape. Combining the improvisation and phrasing material in this level, which revision addresses the request?
questions.answer: Keep the five-note vocabulary but build four-bar phrases that begin and end on chord tones and leave the last beat of each phrase silent, so one quarter of the section carries no notes
questions.distractor: Change the scale when the chord changes, moving to a new position for each harmony, so that the solo follows the chords more closely
questions.correction: The pentatonic already contains the notes needed for both chords, and the listener's complaint is about structure rather than vocabulary: phrases are units that give a sense of completing a formal unit, and continuous eighth notes give the listener no boundary to group. Ending each four-bar phrase with a measured rest supplies that boundary, and four silent beats out of sixty-four is a small change in material with a large change in perceived shape. Changing position at every chord change adds hand movement without adding phrase endings, and the shared tones such as A, C and D would be abandoned at the point where they do the most work.

questions.prompt: A learner records a keyboard part by capturing the instrument's audio output, then wants to correct one wrong note without replaying the part. Which statement about the options is accurate, and what should the learner change next time?
questions.answer: The capture is recorded sound, so the correction means slicing the waveform or replaying the part; next time the keyboard performance should be captured as note data, which can be edited per note without artefacts
questions.distractor: The capture is note data, so the wrong note can simply be dragged to the right pitch and the change will be audible immediately without any further work
questions.correction: Recording filter categories separate Notes, which record note data from keyboards and drum pads, from Audio, which records sound, and an audio capture is a waveform containing the performance as it was played. Correcting a note inside that waveform means cutting and moving a fragment, with the click and envelope risks that editing brings, or replaying the part. Capturing the same performance as note data would allow the note to be moved exactly and reversibly, because what is stored is an instruction to play rather than a recording of sound.

questions.prompt: A learner decides to quantise an audio guitar part by slicing twelve late notes out of the take and moving each onto the grid. Each slice creates two joins, and each join is covered by a fade of about 10 ms. Computed from those numbers, how much fade time does the edit introduce in total, and what is the larger musical risk?
questions.answer: About 240 ms of total fade across twenty-four joins, and the larger risk is that the played timing which carries the groove is being removed rather than repaired
questions.distractor: About 120 ms of total fade across twelve joins, and the larger risk is that the fades will be audible as gaps in the middle of notes
questions.correction: Twelve notes sliced out of a waveform create two joins each, so twenty-four joins, and twenty-four fades of 10 ms total about 240 ms of fade time. The arithmetic matters less than the musical effect: the deviations from the grid are part of the timing that makes a part sound played, and slicing them away converts a performance into a sequence, while each new join also carries the risk of a click if the fade is missed. Where a part needs more than a couple of repairs, the recommended response is to re-record the section rather than to continue slicing.

questions.prompt: A chart handed out at a rehearsal shows a single block of 32 bars with no section labels. Using the conventions for sections and phrases in this level, what is the most useful first observation to raise with the group?
questions.answer: Sections typically span 8 to 24 bars and contain two to four phrases, so 32 unlabelled bars probably contain two or more sections that need labels before anyone counts entries
questions.distractor: Thirty-two bars is the standard length of a single section, so the chart is complete and the group should simply count from one to thirty-two together
questions.correction: The form chapter states that a section typically spans between 8 and 24 bars and includes two to four phrases, and that section boundaries are usually made audible by several simultaneous cues. Thirty-two bars therefore suggests two or more sections whose labels have been omitted, and without those labels a player has no road map for repeats, no phrase boundaries for planning entries, and no basis for the lettering that would describe the form. The observation is not pedantry: unlabelled bars are the commonest cause of a group losing its place together.

questions.prompt: Two rhythm players rehearse a four-bar vamp at 100 beats per minute and both strum on every beat, which sounds loud and vague. A listener suggests giving them different jobs. Using the texture and ensemble material in this level, which assignment is best, and what is the resulting spacing between their attacks?
questions.answer: One plays the backbeat on beats 2 and 4 while the other plays the offbeats on the half-beats, so their attacks alternate about 0.300 s apart
questions.distractor: One plays on beats 1 and 3 while the other doubles beats 2 and 4 an octave higher, so their attacks coincide on every beat but at different pitches
questions.correction: At 100 beats per minute a beat is 0.600 s and a half-beat is 0.300 s, so a backbeat part and an offbeat part interleave with one attack roughly every 0.300 s, giving the ear a continuous rhythmic surface and a clear pulse. Having one player double the other's beats at a different octave leaves every attack coincident, which is the arrangement that exposes both players' timing differences at once and gives the listener no information between downbeats. Dividing the slots is the practical application of the afterbeat and offbeat textures named in the theory sources.

questions.prompt: A learner reports practising 60 minutes without a break, monitoring through headphones loud enough to hear detail, and hearing ringing afterwards, then asks how to make the next session more productive. Which response is consistent with this level's practice and safety guidance?
questions.answer: Shorten the session with breaks, warm up first, set the monitor level once and lower it until the ringing stops, because ringing after a session is a signal that the level was too high rather than a normal outcome
questions.distractor: Keep the long session because total practice time is the main predictor of improvement, and use louder monitoring to hear detail that is otherwise masked
questions.correction: The practice evidence in this level does not support time as the operative variable: retention quality was unrelated to practice time, total trials and complete trials, while the proportion of correct trials was related, so a shorter session with better error control is the productive direction. Separately, hearing is the instrument the judgement depends on, and persistent ringing after monitoring indicates an unsafe level; safe-listening guidance exists precisely because loudness exposure accumulates. Break the session, warm up before demanding playing, and reduce the level rather than the material.

questions.prompt: A player adds the flat fifth to A minor pentatonic to make the blues scale over an Am7 to D7 vamp, then holds that note for a whole bar as the D7 arrives. Using the blues-scale material and the chord-tone reasoning in this level, what is the accurate description of what happened?
questions.answer: The note is a blue note rather than a chord tone, and over D7 it sits a semitone above the root as a flat ninth, so holding it produces a clash where using it as a passing note produces a blues idiom
questions.distractor: The note is a chord tone of both chords, so holding it is always safe and the clash the listener reports must come from the accompaniment being out of balance
questions.correction: The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with an added flat fifth, and the source names the flat third and flat fifth as blue notes because they are not chord tones of a major triad or dominant seventh chord. In A the added note is E flat, which is a semitone below the fifth of Am7 and a semitone above the root of D7, where it functions as a flat ninth. The same pitch used as a passing note between the fourth and the fifth reads as blues; held as a long note against D7 it reads as a clash, so duration and position rather than pitch identity decide the outcome.

questions.prompt: A learner completes the capstone: three complete takes of a 76.8 s part, one chosen, a written reason naming the timing criterion, and a render of the chosen take as a 16-bit stereo WAV at 44.1 kHz. Which package statement is accurate about the deliverable?
questions.answer: The file is about 12.92 MB, computed from 76.8 s at 44.1 kHz stereo and 16 bits, and 16-bit is generally sufficient for distribution while a 24-bit version would be for archiving
questions.distractor: The file is about 38.76 MB because a WAV always contains all recorded takes, and a MIDI copy of the same take would be an equivalent audio deliverable
questions.correction: A 76.8 s stereo 16-bit file at 44.1 kHz is 76.8 x 44100 x 2 channels x 2 bytes, which is about 12.92 MB; 38.76 MB is the size of the three takes together, which a render of the chosen take does not contain. The export documentation states that audio formats save an audio mix while a MIDI file saves note data and is not an audio format, so a MIDI copy is a different kind of object rather than an equivalent deliverable. The bit-depth guidance in the same page is that 16-bit is generally enough for music distribution and that 24 or 32-bit files are for archiving production material.
